item.title: Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models
item.description: <p><a href="https://projectdiscovery.io/research/how-abliterated-models-can-get-you-pwned">This</a> is a problem:</p> <blockquote><p>Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it&#8217;s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it&#8217;s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what&#8217;s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model&#8217;s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries &#8220;no&#8221; and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it&#8217;s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you&#8217;ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI&#8217;s gpt-oss...</p></blockquote>

item.title: Measuring Human Cryptanalysis Effort
item.description: <p>Matthew Green has a <a href="https://bitsofwork.org/">new site</a> that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms:</p> <blockquote><p><b>Abstract:</b> We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work...</p></blockquote>
item.dc:creator: Bruce Schneier
